ap_macroeconomics-m01.stem: Households in an economy decide to save a larger share of their income at every real interest rate. Which statement best describes the effect in the market for loanable funds?

options.text: The supply of loanable funds decreases, so the real interest rate rises and investment falls.
options.why: Higher saving raises the amount of funds offered at each rate, so supply does not fall.

options.text: The demand for loanable funds increases, so the real interest rate rises and investment falls.
options.why: Saving is a source of loanable funds, so it changes supply rather than demand.

options.text: The supply of loanable funds increases, so the equilibrium real interest rate falls and the quantity of investment rises.
options.why: More saving shifts the supply curve right, which lowers the real rate and raises the quantity of funds borrowed for investment.

options.text: The supply of loanable funds increases, so the real interest rate rises and investment falls.
options.why: A rightward supply shift lowers the equilibrium real interest rate.

options.text: Neither curve shifts, so the real interest rate stays the same and investment is unchanged.
options.why: A change in saving at every rate is a shift of the supply curve, not a movement along it.

options.text: The real interest rate and private investment are unchanged, because the government spends the money it borrows.
options.why: The government's borrowing competes with private borrowers for the same funds.

options.text: The real interest rate falls and private investment rises, because government spending adds to the supply of funds.
options.why: Government borrowing draws on funds, so it raises demand rather than supply.

options.text: The real interest rate rises and private investment falls, because government borrowing increases the demand for loanable funds.
options.why: Government borrowing adds to the demand for funds, which raises the real rate and crowds out some private borrowing for investment.

options.text: The real interest rate rises and private investment rises, because higher rates reward savers.
options.why: A higher real rate lowers the quantity of funds firms want to borrow for investment.

options.text: The real interest rate falls and private investment falls, because less saving is available.
options.why: A rate decrease would not accompany an increase in the demand for funds.

options.why: Lower demand for funds leads to a lower, not higher, real interest rate.

options.text: The real interest rate rises and private investment falls, because paying down debt reduces the supply of funds.
options.why: Reduced government borrowing lowers demand for funds, so supply does not fall.

options.text: The real interest rate falls and private investment falls, because lower rates discourage borrowing.
options.why: A lower real rate raises the quantity of funds firms want to borrow for investment.

options.text: The real interest rate falls and private investment rises, because lower government borrowing decreases the demand for loanable funds.
options.why: Less government borrowing shifts demand left, which lowers the real rate and lets more funds go to private investment.

options.text: The equilibrium real interest rate rises and the quantity of loanable funds falls.
options.why: Two rightward shifts cannot lower the equilibrium quantity.

options.text: The equilibrium real interest rate rises, but the change in the quantity cannot be determined.
options.why: When both curves shift right, the quantity changes for certain and the rate is the ambiguous result.

options.text: The equilibrium quantity of loanable funds increases, but the change in the real interest rate cannot be determined.
options.why: Supply and demand both shift right, so quantity rises for sure, while the real rate depends on which shift is larger.

options.why: A rightward demand shift pushes the rate up, so a fall cannot be guaranteed.

options.text: Both the real interest rate and the quantity are unchanged, because the two shifts offset each other.
options.why: The shifts offset in the rate only if they are of exactly the right size, and they still raise the quantity.
